newsitem.title: CANADA: Loewen Group CEO to fight Service to the death.
newsitem.headline: Loewen Group CEO to fight Service to the death.

text.p: In launching a $2.9 billion hostile bid for funeral-home chain Loewen Group Inc., Service Corp. International confronts a formidable opponent in the form of Loewen's iron-willed founder.
Ray Loewen, the company's chairman and chief executive, owns 15 percent of its stock and is considered by analysts to be the biggest obstacle to a takeover.

Loewen Group has not yet formally responded to Houston-based Service's sweetened $45-a-share stock offer announced on Wednesday. But industry insiders and investors widely expect Loewen to wage a battle to the death to keep his company out of Service's grasp.
"He won't back down," said Lawrence Little, a partner in a Canadian funeral company who has known Loewen for years.

Forget the hushed tones and gentle demeanor commonly associated with undertakers. A gregarious one-time funeral director and Bible college graduate, 56-year-old Loewen has shown more than once he is not shy of a nasty fight.

When he took over his family's funeral home in rural Steinbach, Manitoba, in the early 1960s, Loewen swiftly forced out his two brothers. And a Mississippi jury last year found Loewen Group guilty of trying to drive a 125-year-old funeral firm out of business, ordering it to pay hefty damages that nearly drove Loewen Group into bankruptcy.
In an interview this week, Loewen made it clear he is ready to go the distance again this time against Service.
"We came from nowhere in 1984 ... and our company has grown exponentially. That didn't come from simply sitting back," he said. "We are not frightened easily."

Loewen, who likes to refer to himself as a small-town boy, has over the past 12 years used homespun charm and aggressive deals to turn Loewen Group into North America's second biggest funeral home operator after Service.
It has 931 funeral homes and 271 cemeteries and this year alone sealed $1.3 billion in acquisitions.

In its drive, Loewen Group has often competed against Service to acquire independent funeral companies across North America. Even before the takeover bid, Loewen and Service chief Robert Waltrip could barely mask their hostility.
Claiming Loewen's growth prospects are superior if it remains independent, Loewen minced no words in explaining what he thinks is motivating Service's bid.
"They want to get Ray Loewen out of the way," he boomed in his trademark baritone. "They do not like competition." Service, for its part, has denied that accusation.

Loewen said last week when the company's board vehemently rejected Service's initial $43-a-share offer that he could see no sound rationale for combining the two companies even if Service bid up to $52 a share. "It's like trying to mix oil and water," he said.
Analysts say Loewen, a devout Mennonite, can probably count on the board to back him up. It's a handpicked group that includes a rabbi and two Christian clergy.

The current battle with Service is the second time in less than a year that Loewen has fought to save his company. Loewen Group was nearly forced into bankruptcy in January after the Mississippi jury slapped it with a $500 million damage award.

Under pressure from the company's shareholders, Loewen Group settled out of court at the last minute for $135 million in cash and stock despite Loewen's vows to take the case all the way to the Supreme Court. The freefall in Loewen Group's stock after that case is what made it vulnerable to Service.
